name: Baiko brown
lede: Baiko brown is a muted olive-brown from Japan's traditional color list, one of the most frequent named colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: In Japan: Baikōcha
sections.body: The name is written 梅幸茶, romanized Baikōcha, listed among Japan's traditional colors [1]. Who it was named for is undocumented in the sources we have; traditional Japanese color names often carried the stage name of a kabuki actor, and *Baikō* was used as such a name, though we cannot confirm the link here [1]. The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[yellowish-olive]], barely greener [2]. Further out, [[gold-fusion]] and [[citrine-drab]] sit in the same small cluster [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Baiko brown in 2,896 of 23,781 paintings, about 12.2 percent, more common than 94 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 300 of 3,449 paintings, 1.3 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a light tone, in 38 percent of its appearances [3]. Nicolas Lancret used it most: 7 of his 16 paintings here carry it, 4.9 times his peers' rate [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with colors we call Eucalyptus and Gull [3]. The earliest archive match dates to 916, and our sources give no Western first-recorded date for this traditional Japanese name to compare it against [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
